items.abstract: <jats:p>Intergenerational mobility, the extent to which economic status evolves across generations, is central to understanding economic opportunity and social dynamics. Rankrank regression has become the standard tool for measuring intergenerational mobility through a linear relationship, but it may overlook heterogeneous dependence patterns. We introduce distributional rank-rank regression, which provides rank-specific correlations across the distribution of parent and child outcomes. Drawing on quantile-based correlation techniques, our framework comprehensively captures nonlinear mobility patterns, accommodates noncontinuous outcome variables through generalized ranks, and incorporates observed covariates via conditional ranks. We establish the asymptotic properties of the estimator under potential misspecification of the first-stage conditional distributions and propose bootstrap procedures for inference. An empirical application to intergenerational educational mobility in India illustrates the proposed method.</jats:p>
title: Distributional Rank-Rank Regression for Heterogeneous Dependence

items.abstract: <jats:p>Reduced-rank structures arise naturally in many economic and financial models, yet empirical implementations typically treat them as static. This paper introduces the Generalized Autoregressive Reduced-Rank Regression framework, in which reduced-rank coefficient matrices evolve through score-driven updating rules and thus allow low-dimensional structures to evolve over time. The framework nests a range of existing multivariate score-driven specifications as special cases. We investigate conditions for stationarity and invertibility of the score-driven filter and establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator under both statistical and economically motivated identification schemes. The empirical relevance of the framework is illustrated in an asset pricing application in which the dynamic low-rank structure arises from no-arbitrage and factor dimensionality considerations.</jats:p>
title: An Observation-Driven Framework for Dynamic Reduced-Rank Regression

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large-scale health surveys suitable for addiction studies furnish self-reported data that consequently suffer from a form of measurement error called heaping, which statisticians have been grappling with for decades. Also known as digit preference, the aberration is often characterized by spikes at multiples of 10 or 5 upon rounding. To date, methods and software for heaped (and seeped) data have been largely wanting. Identifying three generic problems for simple addiction studies, we solve them by a newly developed technique, called Generally Altered, Inflated, Truncated and Deflated (GAITD) regression, for counts applied to a recent National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data set. In conjunction, we propose the class of doubly constrained reduced-rank VGLMs whereby the reduced-rank regression is afforded structure by way of linear constraints—this allows further simplification of the dimension reduction. We determine the distribution of smoking initiation age (SIA) and its association with tobacco consumption and smoking duration; for example, is a lower SIA associated with higher tobacco consumption later in life? Is higher SIA associated with shorter smoking duration among quitters? Together, GAITD regression and DRR-VGLMs hold promise for heaped and seeped data.</jats:p>
title: Heaping and seeping, GAITD regression and doubly constrained reduced-rank vector generalized linear models in smoking studies

items.abstract: <jats:p>We develop a sparse Bayesian regularization framework for reduced-rank predictive regression, extending the global-local view of regularization (Polson and Sokolov, 2019) from coordinate-wise sparsity to two new structures: the spectral directions of an ill-conditioned design and the rank of the predictive coefficient. Starting from the regularized reducedrank regression (RRRR) objective of Dobrev and Schaumburg (2014), we show that its filter factors are exactly the per-direction posterior shrinkage weights, so that Tikhonov ridge and spectral truncation are the constant-variance and spike-and-slab endpoints of a single Gaussian-prior family. The mean-square-optimal filter is an oracle posterior mean depending on an unknown per-direction signal-to-noise ratio; a horseshoe prior on the singular directions provides its feasible, data-adaptive surrogate, and a column-wise global-local prior on the factor loadings selects the number of forecasting factors automatically. The construction is conditionally conjugate, links directly to sparse deep learning as regularized regression (Polson and Sokolov, 2017), and reduces to RRRR in the fixed-scale, fixedrank limit. A Monte Carlo study calibrated to Dobrev and Schaumburg (2014) confirms that (i) the horseshoe posterior filter tracks the oracle filter while ridge over-smooths and truncation is brittle; (ii) the reduced-rank horseshoe matches oracle-tuned RRRR in outof-sample mean-squared error without selecting either the number of components or the rank; and (iii) column shrinkage recovers the true number of forecasting factors. On the FRED-MD macroeconomic panel-the modern Stock-Watson diffusion-index problemthe method beats an autoregressive benchmark for almost every aggregate, matches the principal-component forecast, and additionally returns calibrated predictive densities, a time-varying number of forecasting factors, and an interpretable factor decomposition.</jats:p>
title: Sparse Reduced-Rank Regression: From Tikhonov to Horseshoe
